title: Jeremy Bentham

cards.h: Utility as the test of law
cards.b:
Jeremy Bentham (1748-1832) founded utilitarianism: the test of any law, act or institution is whether it adds to human happiness. It is the basis of modern policy analysis, cost-benefit thinking and welfare economics, and also a major target of liberal and Rawlsian critics.

Expect this as a 10 or 15 mark question, or as a supporting example inside a longer answer. Read the cards in order, then test yourself with the quiz.

In An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation (1789) Bentham opens: 'Nature has placed mankind under the governance of two sovereign masters, pain and pleasure.' The principle of utility approves actions that increase the greatest happiness of the greatest number.

Each person counts as one, nobody for more than one. This gives a democratic, equal base.
He thought happiness can be measured and compared. The 'hedonic calculus' is a rough guide for lawmakers.

Bentham rejected natural rights as fiction. Rights are created by law, and 'natural and imprescriptible rights' are 'nonsense upon stilts' (Anarchical Fallacies). He is thus a legal positivist: law is command of the sovereign, not moral truth. This undercuts both Locke and the French Declaration.

Bentham pressed for law reform: codification, prison and poor-law reform, secret ballot, wider suffrage, and rights for women and animals (he asked of animals, 'The question is not, Can they reason? nor, Can they talk? but, Can they suffer?'). The Panopticon (1791) is a circular prison where inmates can be watched at any time without seeing the watcher, later made famous by Foucault.

Bentham began as an adviser to enlightened rulers, but after 1809 he became a radical democrat. In Plan of Parliamentary Reform (1817) and the Constitutional Code he urged universal suffrage, secret ballot, annual elections and the removal of the Lords. His reason: rulers pursue sinister interests, so the many must watch the few. His followers, the Philosophic Radicals, helped pass the Reform Act 1832, and University College London (1826) reflects his secular ideals.

• J.S. Mill: pleasures differ in quality, so 'better Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied'.
  • Rawls: utilitarianism ignores the separateness of persons and could sacrifice a minority.
  • Happiness is hard to measure and compare.
  • Defenders: it is impartial, practical and reformist.

In an answer, give two points for and two against, then close with a balanced verdict. Examiners reward a clear stand backed by a named thinker or case.

Act utilitarians judge each act by its results. Rule utilitarians judge general rules by their results, which protects rights better. Modern forms: preference utilitarianism (Peter Singer), welfare economics and cost-benefit analysis in policy.

Keep the name, the year and the one-line claim ready. These three details are what examiners look for when they check a concept.

Utilitarians shaped colonial policy. James Mill wrote History of British India (1817) and worked at the East India Company; Macaulay drafted the Indian Penal Code (1837, in force 1860), influenced by Benthamite codification. Raja Ram Mohan Roy corresponded with Bentham. Critics argue that utility served as a justification for paternal, authoritarian rule. Modern echoes: cost-benefit tests for projects, and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (2023) as a codification update.
